title: The reading map — what to read next, in order
desc: Where to go after the Path: which translations, which monographs, which primary texts in which order — and what to avoid, with the reason stated.
tldr: The last step is a map out of here. Four tiers: the translation to own, the primary texts in reading order, the monographs that will change how you read them, and the things to skip. Everything named with its edition, because an edition is the difference between reading a source and reading someone's idea of it.
body:
You have read a source, learned the concept map, taken apart the most quoted line, followed the tradition from Roman Egypt to Chicago. This step tells you what to do next, in order, with the reasons.

Tier 1: the one book to own

Brian P. Copenhaver, Hermetica (Cambridge University Press, 1992). The Corpus Hermeticum and the Asclepius in modern English, with an introduction and notes that are worth the price on their own. If you buy one book, buy this. Every quotation on this site is checked against it.

For the Greek and a fuller apparatus, the standard critical edition remains Nock and Festugière's Corpus Hermeticum (1945–54), in Greek with French translation. M. David Litwa's Hermetica II (Cambridge UP, 2018) collects the fragments and testimonia that Copenhaver does not include.

Tier 2: the primary texts, in reading order

1. Poimandres (CH I). The vision, the cosmogony, the doubled human, the ascent. Start here; you already have a guided walkthrough.

2. CH XIII, on rebirth. The transformation staged as a dialogue between Hermes and his son, with the vices leaving one by one. The most practical text in the collection.

3. The Asclepius. Survives in Latin; contains the famous lament for Egypt and the passage on god-making statues that got the tradition into trouble.

4. The Emerald Tablet. Twelve lines; read them after CH I so you can see what changed between Greek philosophy and Arabic technical literature.

5. The Discourse on the Eighth and Ninth (NHC VI,6). A Coptic ritual text found at Nag Hammadi, showing the practical side the philosophical treatises only imply.

Tier 3: the monographs that change your reading

Garth Fowden, The Egyptian Hermes (1986). Puts the texts in Roman Egypt and argues the philosophical and technical Hermetica belong to one milieu. Still the best single account of the world that produced them.

Kevin van Bladel, The Arabic Hermes (2009). How Hermes travelled through the Islamic world — the stage most European accounts skip entirely, and the one that produced the Emerald Tablet.

Christian H. Bull, The Tradition of Hermes Trismegistus (2018). The most recent major reassessment; argues for a real priestly milieu behind the texts.

Wouter J. Hanegraaff, Esotericism and the Academy (2012). Not about Hermeticism specifically, but about how the whole category was constructed — the book that makes you sceptical in a useful direction.

Frances A. Yates, Giordano Bruno and the Hermetic Tradition (1964). Read it for the Renaissance chapters and for its historical importance, with the knowledge that its central thesis is now considered overstated.

Tier 4: what to skip, and why

The Kybalion as a source on antiquity. Fine as a document of 1908; see step 10.

Anything promising decoded alchemical recipes. The texts use deliberate cover names; anyone claiming a clean decoding owes you their verification method, and almost nobody has one.

Free online 'complete Hermetica' of unclear provenance. Usually Mead 1906 or Everard 1650, reformatted without saying so. Both are public domain and worth reading as historical documents — just know that you are reading a pre-critical translation, and prefer our hub, which says which is which.

And then

If you want the tradition as a working practice rather than a subject, that is what our book and the practice tool are for — with the seam between the sources and our application kept visible throughout. If you want to keep reading history, follow tier 3 and then the footnotes; that is how the field actually works.

One translation, five texts, five monographs, three things to skip. That is the whole map, and it fits in a note on your phone.
facts: CH I → CH XIII → Asclepius → Emerald Tablet → NHC VI,6
Everard 1650, Mead 1906 — historical documents, not standards
faq: No. Copenhaver's translation is designed for readers without it, and his notes flag the places where the Greek is doing something a translation cannot carry. Learn the vocabulary of the debates instead — that is where the real difficulty lives.
What if I only have an hour a week?

Then read CH I once a month and let it work. This is short literature written to be reread; the second and third passes give more than the first, and no amount of secondary reading substitutes for knowing one primary text well.
Where do the Polish readers go?

The scholarship is overwhelmingly in English, French and German. Polish-language editions exist but are uneven; the honest advice is to read Copenhaver in English if you can, and to treat any Polish popular edition without an editorial apparatus with the same caution as any other.
sources: Copenhaver (1992), Nock & Festugière (1945–54), Litwa (2018) — the editions named above.
Fowden (1986), van Bladel (2009), Bull (2018), Hanegraaff (2012), Yates (1964).
